MN202611_1yioyz2hvfw.t:
Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officer

Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

Psychologist Sebastian Lundström runs the clinic, which operates one day a month

Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.

When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.

Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.

Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.

"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.

The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.

But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.

"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.

"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."

Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.

During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.

"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."

It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.

"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.

"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.

The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.

"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."

In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.

Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions

The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.

"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.

Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.

Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.

Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.

People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.

Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".

"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.

Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.

The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.

Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.

She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.

"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

MN202611_125g80c94h6.t:
Health officials are urging more people to take up the offer of a free flu vaccine as the number of hospital patients seriously ill with the virus has risen sharply in the past week.

The flu surge has come slightly early this year but that is not completely unusual.

Flu activity is still at "moderate levels" and the peak may not arrive until December or early January, health officials warn.

So what is the advice on getting a vaccine, who can get it for free and who should pay?

"If you're offered it, it's a good idea to have it," says Prof Nick Hopkinson, professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London.

"The main reason is to avoid serious complications in vulnerable groups – so as many as possible should have it in those groups.

"People don't understand it's a potentially life-threatening infection and that the vaccine is safe."

Flu is a viral infection which affects the nose, throat and lungs. Often it goes away on its own but it can make people seriously ill – complications can include pneumonia, heart attacks and other underlying illnesses getting worse.

In England last winter, UKHSA estimated there were 3,798 deaths attributed to influenza.

Scientists have to predict which strains of influenza will be circulating before the vaccine is manufactured each year in time for winter.

The current one protects against three strains – two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.

Even if these strains drift slightly, experts say getting vaccinated is still a good idea to lower the risk of severe illness.

Millions of vulnerable people are eligible for the free jab to help protect them against flu, including children, pregnant women, care home residents, people with lung conditions and anyone aged 65 and over.

But only around a third of under-65s and two-thirds of those aged 65 and over have been vaccinated so far this winter.

That leaves around seven million people unprotected at present, health officials say.

Parents are being urged to vaccinate young children in order to protect them and other people they come into contact with.

Yes. The vaccine does not rule out the possibility you will get flu, but it does reduce the chances you'll become very ill with it and end up in hospital.

It takes two weeks for your body's immunity to build up after being vaccinated, which is another reason to have the jab sooner rather than later.

Protection from the vaccine reduces the risk of serious flu complications by 50%, says Prof Hopkinson.

If you are not eligible for the free flu vaccine, you can still buy it from most pharmacies for between £15 and 25.

"It's a reasonable thing to consider," says Prof Hopkinson.

But it is far more important for the millions of vulnerable people offered it free to be vaccinated.

They are known to be at risk of health complications from the virus.

Other groups are also at risk: "Smokers are five times more likely to get flu – so quit now," he suggests.

There are different vaccines for those getting it free on the NHS and those paying for it privately.

However, the vaccines do the same job and protect against the same strains of flu.

Pharmacist Olivier Picard says he's seen a "massive spike in demand" for flu jabs in the last 24 hours.

More people are booking an appointment for a free vaccine they have already been reminded about, and others are asking about paying for it themselves.

"When it gets cold, people tend to wake up to getting the free jab and want it before Christmas," he says.

He says there is no issue with supplies of the vaccine at present and "plenty in the system".

Vithabhai Narayangaonkar was a legend in Maharashtra's folk theatre

Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.

Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.

In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.

"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.

Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"

When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.

"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.

Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.

Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.

Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.

"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.

Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.

It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.

Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.

Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.

Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.

Vithabai was known as the empress of Tamasha in Maharashtra

Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.

At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.

There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.

In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.

When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.

Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.

Despite drawing huge crowds, Lavni dancers were often disdained

Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.

Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.

Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.

Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.

Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.

Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.

Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.

"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.

But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.

"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

MN202611_xg84xr11el.t:
Grand Theft Auto 6 saw record retail sales in its first full day of release, hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history

Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem – and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.

The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch – 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.

This time it may not have that luxury – in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.

These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6

Barely a week after the release of GTA 6, efforts are already under way to get an unofficial version playable on PC, although some projects have faced takedown notices from the game's publisher.

For some gamers, it's an exciting prospect, despite the legal questions surrounding the process.

For developers, it may be a warning: if a game as big as GTA 6 can be recreated, what does that mean for everyone else?

The recent wave of AI-assisted game recreation has been widely linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code.

Mark Brown, creator of the YouTube channel Game Maker's Toolkit and whose own game Word Play was recently recreated using AI, said cloning largely took two forms: replication and reverse engineering.

Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one, possibly using screenshots or a description.

This, he said, was similar to "looking at a painting and making your own replica" – something which is "a very close copy, but is ultimately a new painting".

It's a particular issue among smaller studios, many of whom worry that AI makes it easier for others to copy their work.

When indie developers Sodoj and Marco from the studio Robotonic noticed a version of their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appear on the free games platform Yandex with the same name, they were "appalled".

"The game was essentially the exact same idea, the exact same mechanics as we had, but with the art looking a bit off," Marco told the BBC .

The duo were able to issue a copyright strike to Yandex and Google to get the copy taken down, but said it only felt like a "small victory".

Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one

The second approach – reverse engineering – involves working backwards from a finished game to understand how it was created.

One way of doing this is decompilation, which attempts to turn the game's final version into something closer to its original source code.

Brown compares the process to "taking a cake and somehow turning it back into the original recipe, with the exact quantities of flour, eggs, and milk used, so anyone can remake the same cake".

Reverse-engineering projects have helped bring games such as Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers.

A related technique, recompilation, can help adapt a game that has been reverse-engineered to run on different hardware. This is one of the methods being explored in efforts to get GTA 6 onto PC.

Coders wanting to attempt this with Rockstar's latest game face a difficult task because of its sheer size and complexity.

Earlier in November, Cyberleek – a hacker or group of hackers – released what they claimed to be a near-complete Xbox development build of the game. They later leaked what they claimed to be the missing .exe file needed to launch the game.

It gave those working on an unofficial PC version a crucial new starting point.

"Now people are using AI to try and decompile it, make a modified version that could run on PC, and compile a new version," said Brown.

Reverse-engineering projects have made it possible to bring full games such as Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers

Since the leak, several groups have posted claims of their progress on platforms such as X, ranging from getting the game to boot up to making it run at a stable rate.

One attempt seen by the BBC on X purported to have some of the game running nearly as smoothly as it does on console, albeit on a high-end PC.

Accounts and sites have even sprung up to track the various attempts, excitedly sharing clips of the latest milestone passed and scoring their efforts.

Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, have not confirmed the authenticity of the leaked build, and neither has responded to the BBC's request for a statement.

However, Take-Two has issued take , external down notices , external of public projects aiming to port the Xbox version to PC on platforms such as GitHub.

"There are no remedies available to rectify this clear attempt to facilitate copyright infringement based upon Take-Two's copyrighted property," one notice stated.

Laura Cress talks to game designers who say their unreleased new game was copied using AI. And Shiona McCallum reports on a new AI police chatbot.

News of the leak has been celebrated by some gamers on Reddit, who resent having to wait for the PC release.

"Why should the PC players have to wait half a year if you can develop the game in weeks as shown so far!" wrote one gamer , external .

"Will be funny when the decomp runs way better than whatever Rockstar can make," said another.

Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said part of the reason why the games are often released on PCs months after consoles is that PC versions are "complex" with "different hardware configurations", as opposed to the more standardised set-up of consoles.

He added there could also be a more commercial reason, as Rockstar can "have a second moment when the PC version is ready".

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal , external , the chief executive of Take-Two Interactive, Strauss Zelnick, said while piracy was a "fact of life" in the entertainment business, it had until now been "less of an issue" for video games due to their "file sizes and complexity".

However, Zelnick also reportedly told an investor Q&A that the company was "utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and... legal activities appropriately".

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics

Dr Tommy Thompson, an AI consultant who presents the AI and Games YouTube channel, said the practice of decompilation exists in a "grey area" until it "reaches a point where copyright and intellectual property [IP] are infringed upon".

He added that decompiling code could be legal within limits, such as for educational purposes, but "as soon as you attempt to use it to redistribute or repackage existing software", then this is "largely illegal".

"In most cases, decompiling or recompiling code is likely to involve unauthorised use of the game IP," said Aaron Treble, a UK intellectual property lawyer for Lewis Silkin.

Anyone who releases or sells a clone "will almost certainly be infringing [on copyright]", Treble added, though he said the law on AI companies' own responsibility is still evolving.

Anthropic has reportedly since told Claude Code to steer away from recreating specific existing games , external , saying this would breach its usage policy.

Despite this, people are continuing to work on an unofficial PC game, hoping to make it playable before Rockstar releases the official version.

"Seeing as this has already affected industry giants with very deep pockets, the proverbial bear has been poked," said Brown.

MN202611_1aicgiy5czs.t:
For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.

He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.

Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.

Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.

The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.

She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.

"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.

The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.

"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.

With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.

Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.

Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.

From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.

Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.

Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.

Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.

He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.

He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.

"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.

Pete Edochie starred in Netflix's first original Nigerian film, Lionheart

His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.

The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.

He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.

His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.

For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.

But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.

Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.

"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."

Edochie's expressions were sometimes used as online memes

Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.

Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.

"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.

"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."

Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.

"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.

"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."

Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.

The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.

But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.

Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.

"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.

He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.

"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.

Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.

Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.

In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.

It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

MN202611_t43mklwj1f.t:
Sentare y'i Mombasa, muri Kenya, yakubise intahe mu gahanga Paul Mackenzie, umukuru w'urushengero rw'abizera ko isi igiye kurangira, ku caha co kwica abayoboke biwe 123 atabigambiriye.

Paul Mackenzie yagiriwe n'icaha co gutegeka abayoboke biwe, bose bakuze, kwisonzesha gushika bapfuye, ivyabereye mw'ishamba rya Shakahola, riri hafi y'inkengera z'ikiyaga, hagati ya Nzero (1) 2021 na Nyakanga (9) 2023.

Mu ntango z'uku kwezi, Mackenzie yari yakatiwe gupfungwa imyaka 200, yagirizwa kwica abantu 191, hafi nka bose bakaba bari abana, mu bwicanyi nk'ubwo nyene bw'ikivunga.

Mackenzie yari yahakanye ivyo yagirizwa ko yishe abantu atabigambiriye. Umwe mu bamwunganira yavuze ko azokwunguruza urubanza, nk'uko bimenyeshwa n'itororokanirizo ry'amakuru Reuters.

Kugabisha: Iyi nkuru irimwo ibishobora kubabaza canke guhungabanya bamwe mu bayisoma.

Sentare yakubise intahe mu gahanga abandi bantu 29, harimwo umugore wa Mackenzie, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, ku ruhara bagize mu mpfu zatewe no gusaba abantu kwisonzesha gushika bapfuye.

Mu bakurikiranwa, 60 barejejwe baca bararekurwa. Uwuserukira ubushikirizamanza yavuze ko bagiye kwunguruza kuri iyo ngingo ya sentare yo kubarekura.

Uwo yiyita umukozi w'Imana yafashwe mu 2023, inyuma y'uko hatowe ibiziga vy'abantu birenga 400 mu mva zari zimbwe mu buryo budashemeye kandi zigera hafi, mw'ishamba rya Shakahola, hafi y'inkengera z'ibahari Indiyano.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Sentare yasanze Mackenzie "yagumye yumvisha abayoboke biwe ko bokwisonzesha gushika bapfuye", nk'uko vyashikirijwe n'Ibiro vy'Ubushikirizamanza ku wa gatanu, aho vyashimangiye ko iri ari "ikubitwa ry'intahe mu gahanga ryiwe rya nyuma" mu manza akurikiranwamwo.

Ivyo biro vyavuze biti: "Abana ni bo bategerezwa kubanza gupfa, bagakurikirwa n'abagore, hanyuma abagabo, Mackenzie na we akaba yari kuzopfa inyuma ya bose."

Ubushikirizamanza bwavuze ko Mackenzie n'abo bakorana bari bafadikanije mu mugambi wo kwiyahura, biciye mu kwisonzesha gushika bapfuye, kugira ngo "bahure na Yezu".

Ababibonye bariko barasura imbere ya sentare, bavuze ko Mackenzie yigisha ko amashure, imiti, n'ibisharizo vyo ku mubiri ari ivyaha.

Nk'uko vyavuzwe mu ngingo y'urubanza rwiwe aho yagirizwa kwica abantu 191, abatemera izo nyigisho ziwe barakubitwa gushika bapfuye.

Abakurikiranwa bavuze ko abo bantu bapfuye bari bisonzesheje ku bushake bwabo.

Mu ntango z'iyi ndwi, Mackenzie kandi yakubiswe intahe mu gahanga kuri ibi:

• Gukubita no gukomeretsa ku mubiri, hamwe n'ibindi vyaha bitanu vyo gufata nabi umwana,

• Kwifatanya n'ibikorwa vy'ubugizi bwa nabi vyateguwe,

• Gufasha mu gutegura canke gushigikira igikorwa c'iterabwoba,

• Gutunga ikintu gifitaniye isano n'icaha, hisunzwe Itegeko rya Kenya ryo mu 2012 rirwanya iterabwoba.

Mackenzie yashinze ishengero ryitwa Good News International Ministries mu 2003. Mu myaka 16 yakurikiye, ryarushirije kumenyekana no gukundwa, rikwegera abayoboke ibihumbi mu mashami yaryo yari hirya no hino muri Kenya.

Imboneshakure Times TV yarashikiriza inyigisho ziwe, zatangirwa mw'ishengero ryiwe riri mu gisagara ca Malindi.

Mu nyigisho ziwe zijanye n'"umuhero w'isi", Mackenzie yavuga ko amashure ari "ikintu kibi", ko kwivuza "binyuranye n'inyigisho z'idini", hamwe n'uko ikarata ndangamuntu z'ubuhinga bwa none ari "ikimenyetso ca shetani".

Inyuma y'uko ishengero rikuru ryugawe mu 2019, Mackenzie yimukiye mw'ishamba rya Shakahola, aho yahimiriza abayoboke biwe kumukurikira.

Baba mu tuzu tw'ivyondo dukwiragiye muri iryo shamba.

Peter Shukrani, umwe mu barokotse, yagize ati: "Twabaho ubuzima busanzwe kandi butekanye, tukamara imisi mikeyi twisonzesheje, hanyuma tugafungura utwo kurya dukeya."

Igihe hatorwa imva bahambwemwo, abagabo bo muri ako karere ni bo bahawe akazi ko kuzura no gukurayo ibiziga vy'abo bantu, igikorwa cari giteye ubwoba.

James, umwe mu babakuyeyo yabwiye BBC ati: "Imva yose twatora, wasanga irimwo ibiziga vy'abantu n'imiburiburi bitatu. Bimwe muri vyo vyari ivy'abana bari bamaze indwi nkeya gusa bavutse."

Yongeyeko ati: "Hari igihe twigeze gutora ibiziga vy'abana 12 biri ku murongo mu mva imwe. Iyo mva yari nini cane, ibiziga vyari bigerekeranye nk'impuzu zizinze, kimwe hejuru y'ikindi."

Abafurura izo mva bavuga ko hari ibiziga vy'abana wasanga "amaboko n'amaguru aboshe, imibiri yabo na yo itekewe mu mashuka".

Ivyegeranyo vy'amasuzuma yakorewe ibiziga inyuma y'urupfu vyerekanye ko benshi mu bapfuye bahitanywe n'inzara. Ibiziga vya bamwe vyari vyarasangutse hasigaye amagufa gusa, ku buryo bitashobotse ko hamenyekana icatumye bapfa.

Stephen Mwiti, afise imyaka 48, yavuze ko yatakaje abana biwe bose uko ari batandatu kubera iryo shengero. Uwahoze ari umugore wiwe ni umwe mu bagiriwe n'icaha co kwica abantu, hamwe na Mackenzie.

Mu kwezi guheze, Mwiti, ari hanze ya sentare, yabwiye BBC ati: "Ndanezerewe no kubona bose bakubiswe intahe mu gahanga."

Yongeyeko ati: "Abana banje bose uko ari batandatu bapfiriye mw'ishamba rya Shakahola. Umwana umwe gusa, Samuel, ni we natoye ibisigarira vy'umubiri wiwe, ndabihamba."

Impfu z'abo bantu zashize ahabona ukuntu ibikorwa vy'amadini yataye umurongo bitagenzurwa neza, n'ukuntu bishobora kubandanya bikamara igihe kirekire ata nkomanzi.

Uburemere bw'uru rubanza bwatumye Perezida William Ruto ashinga umurwi ujejwe gutohoza ivyabaye, n'ubwo mu nyuma wahavuye utangazwa ko ishirwaho ryawo ritisunze ibwirizwa nshingiro.

MN202611_g3ho99akq3.t:
A Peruvian military helicopter crashed during a rescue mission

Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.

Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.

The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.

In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".

It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".

The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.

No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".

In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.

Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine , according to the United Nations.

Cafer Mahiroğlu says Halk TV has been "destroyed" by Turkish authorities

Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.

Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.

In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.

Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.

Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.

"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month , halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.

The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom , external , though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.

However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.

Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.

Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws , which he and his party have fiercely denied.

Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

Pharmacies are being given more freedom over the prescription medicines they can give to patients when items are out of stock.

Staff will be able to offer the same drug in a different strength or form – two 5mg tablets in the place of a 10mg pill, or a cream instead of an ointment, for example.

The change should help patients avoid repeat trips to their GP for an alternative prescription when the issue can be resolved safely and easily at the chemist.

And for the first time, children in England who miss their flu vaccination at school will be able to receive it at a pharmacy instead.

For decades, pharmacists have usually had to provide exactly the medicine prescribed by a doctor under rules set out in the 1968 Medicines Act.

If a product was out of stock, patients often had to return to their GP for an alternative prescription or wait for new supplies to arrive, if it was safe to do so.

Now, pharmacists will be able to make some tweaks without sending patients back to the doctor, including:

supplying the same dose of a drug in different strength pills

supplying the same medicine in a different form, such as a capsule rather than a solid tablet

The changes will apply across the UK once they have been approved by the relevant parliaments and assemblies.

Public health minister Diana Johnson said the new flexibility would make life easier for patients.

"When you go to the pharmacy to pick up your prescription, there is nothing worse than being told you need to contact your GP again because the exact medicine they've prescribed isn't available at that time, or in that form," she said.

"That's why we're changing the rules so that people can get the treatment they need with less hassle, and no delay."

The move follows a broader expansion of pharmacy services in England, which has given pharmacists greater powers to prescribe certain medications themselves without patients needing to see a GP at all.

That scheme now covers 12 common conditions:

Many other medicines, like certain painkillers and cold remedies, can also be bought over the counter at pharmacies without a prescription.

Henry Gregg from the National Pharmacy Association welcomed the move, but called for more action on drug shortages which he said were becoming endemic.

"These measures are a step forward but do not fix the underlying causes of shortages," he added.

"It's clear the government undervalues medicines, including underfunding vital local pharmacies.

"It must take action so that manufacturers don't favour other countries when stocks are low internationally."

The changes are separate from existing powers used during widespread medicine shortages.

If the government is concerned about national stocks of a particular medicine or medical product, it can still issue a Serious Shortage Protocol , external .

The measure has previously been used during shortages of some hormone replacement therapy (HRT) products, for example.

In those circumstances, pharmacists can already dispense an alternative without having to contact a GP first.
